title: Deco and Depression
tagline: Talking pictures, sliced bread and new skyscrapers, as the Depression deepens.

locale.persona: an office clerk's family in New York City

morningRoutine.detail: The 1930 census counted radios in about 12 million homes, 40% of all households.

source.label: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970, series R 93–105: households with radio and television sets

morningRoutine.detail: Pre-sliced, wrapped bread was new. Wonder Bread was one of the first sold sliced nationwide by 1930.

source.label: Wikipedia: Sliced bread

morningRoutine.detail: Unemployment had jumped from 3.2% in 1929 to 8.7% in 1930, more than 4 million people, so the job pages were read closely.

source.label: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970, series D 85–86: unemployment

morningRoutine.detail: A ride of any length on the subway or elevated trains cost a nickel, as it had since 1904.

source.label: Wikipedia: New York City transit fares

morningRoutine.detail: Skyscrapers were rising across Manhattan; the Chrysler Building was completed in May 1930.

source.label: Wikipedia: Chrysler Building

technology.name: Household radio
technology.description: Census figures counted a radio in 40% of households in 1930; it was the family's news, music and serials.

source.label: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970, series R 93–105: households with radio and television sets

technology.name: Ford Model A
technology.description: Ford's successor to the Model T; two million had been sold by July 1929.

source.label: Wikipedia: Ford Model A (1927–1932)

technology.name: Clear cellophane tape
technology.description: Richard Drew developed the first transparent sticky tape in St. Paul, Minnesota, in 1930.

source.label: Wikipedia: Scotch tape

technology.name: Bread-slicing machine
technology.description: Sliced, wrapped bread arrived in 1928 and spread nationwide by 1930.

source.label: Wikipedia: Sliced bread

technology.name: Talking pictures
technology.description: Studios had stopped making purely silent features, though many films still came in silent versions for theatres not yet wired for sound.

source.label: Wikipedia: Sound film

technology.name: Electric refrigerator
technology.description: Sold since 1915 and catching on during the 1930s, the electric refrigerator was starting to replace the icebox.

source.label: Wikipedia: Refrigerator

futureVisions.prediction: A hundred years from now, rising productivity may let people work three-hour shifts, a fifteen-hour week.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: John Maynard Keynes, "Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren", 1930
futureVisions.note: Not on track: full-time work weeks are still far longer than fifteen hours, four years before his deadline.

source.label: John Maynard Keynes, "Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren" (1930), full text (Yale course reader)

futureVisions.prediction: In a hundred years the standard of living in progressive countries will be between four and eight times as high as it is today.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: John Maynard Keynes, "Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren", 1930
futureVisions.note: U.S. real GDP per person rose from about $8,800 in 1930 to about $69,700 in 2025 (2017 dollars), almost eight times as high.

source.label: John Maynard Keynes, "Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren" (1930), full text (Yale course reader)

futureVisions.prediction: Humans will one day redesign their own species by deliberately changing heredity.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: Olaf Stapledon, Last and First Men, a "future history" novel published 23 October 1930
futureVisions.note: Gene editing now exists: the first CRISPR therapy was approved in 2023, for sickle cell disease. Redesigning the species has not happened.

source.label: Wikipedia: Last and First Men
